new_statements.quote: Some support for the first claim comes from DiCanio et al. (2018), who argue for fixed final stress in Yoloxóchitl Mixtec. [...] Additionally, in their typology of Mixtec stress patterns DiCanio and Bennett (2020) include seven languages with root-initial stress, as well as four with final stress and three with variable stress. So, despite the fact that some Mixtec languages have been argued to have final stress, there is no typological basis for claiming that is a common feature of Mixtec languages. More work needs to be done to determine the stress pattern of SMPM.13 [...] In fact, neither word appears to be more prominent, which may indicate that ϕ are unheaded in the language. [fn. 13:] It is possible that the general restriction of rising tones to word final position is indicative of final stress in the language. However, I don't think this is the only possible explanation.
new_statements.citation: Hedding, Andrew A. 2022. How to Move a Focus: The Syntax of Alternative Particles. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Cruz (September 2022), §3.5.3 'Against right-headed prominence'.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. Opened (309-page PDF, XeTeX, Aug 2022) and extracted PDF pp. 184-189 with extracted text. The quoted passage is there verbatim at printed pp. 176-177 (PDF pp. 186-187), under the run-in heading 'Against right-headed prominence' inside §3.5.3 'Focus prominence is not "default" prominence' (TOC p. 171): 'Some support for the first claim comes from DiCanio et al. (2018), who argue for fixed final stress in Yoloxóchitl Mixtec. However, it should be noted that the towns of San Martín Peras and Yoloxóchitl are roughly 100 miles apart... Additionally, in their typology of Mixtec stress patterns DiCanio and Bennett (2020) include seven languages with root-initial stress, as well as fou…
new_statements.rule_in_words: San Martín Peras Mixtec (the west2643 dialect all modern phonology treats) is a tone language (H, M, L, LH, HL; mora = TBU) with a right-aligned bimoraic foot (the 'couplet'); no source assigns a word-stress position. Hedding 2022 states outright that the stress pattern of SMPM remains to be determined: final stress is 'plausible' (rising tones are confined to the word-final position) but not established, and phrase-level prominence is not rightmost-headed. Eischens & Bennett 2025 (lingbuzz p. 13) likewise leave open 'whether feet are taken to be trochaic or iambic in SMP Mixtec', i.e. whether the stressed mora is the penultimate or the final one of the foot. The only measured prominence (Hedding 2021) is focus-driven pitch raising of a word-final High tone with no durational correlate.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Hedding's fn. 13 offers a historical (sandhi-fossilization) explanation for final-position rising tones as an alternative to final stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/couplet level: Hedding's discussion concerns the final syllable within the word vs. the rightmost word within the phrase; his phrase-level test (noun + adjective, 64 sentences) found no difference in H-tone pitch between the two words. Eischens & Bennett discuss the foot within the prosodic word (roots plus vocalic enclitics).
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted material describes San Martín Peras Mixtec (Glottolog dialect sanm1291 of west2643; Ethnologue places it in jmx; Eischens & Hedding's consultants are from Ahuejutla and the San Martín Peras cabecera). The San Juan Piñas sources (sanj1280 in Glottolog) self-identify with ISO vmc, so their assignment to west2643 rests on Glottolog, not on the authors. The Silacayoapan Mixtec items Glottolog lists under west2643 (Shields 1988; North & Shields 1976/1977) describe a separate language (sila1250, ISO mks). No source of any kind was found for the Coicoyán (coic1238) dialect beyond the unopened Beatham & Beatham 2019 orthography proposal.

sources.quote: Some support for the first claim comes from DiCanio et al. (2018), who argue for fixed final stress in Yoloxóchitl Mixtec. [...] Additionally, in their typology of Mixtec stress patterns DiCanio and Bennett (2020) include seven languages with root-initial stress, as well as four with final stress and three with variable stress. So, despite the fact that some Mixtec languages have been argued to have final stress, there is no typological basis for claiming that is a common feature of Mixtec languages. More work needs to be done to determine the stress pattern of SMPM.13 [...] In fact, neither word appears to be more prominent, which may indicate that ϕ are unheaded in the language. sources.note: §3.5.3 'Against right-headed prominence', pp. 176–177 + fn. 13: cites DiCanio et al. 2018 (final stress in Yoloxóchitl) and DiCanio & Bennett's Mixtec typology (7 root-initial, 4 final, 3 variable), concludes 'More work needs to be done to determine the stress pattern of SMPM'; final stress 'plausible' (rising tones restricted to word-final position) but offered an alternative historical explanation 'without appealing to word stress'; no evidence that the rightmost word in a phrase is more prominent (ϕ possibly unheaded).

sources.citation: Caballero, Gabriela, Claudia Duarte Borquez, Claudia Juárez Chávez & Michelle Yuan. 2026. Lexical and grammatical tone in San Juan Piñas Mixtec (Tò'ōn Ndá'ví). Phonological Data and Analysis 8, e7: 1–36. doi:10.1017/S2642182825000029
sources.note: §3.2 (p. 5): 'We assume that this bimoraic phonological unit is equivalent to a metrical foot, aligned at the right edge of a prosodic word'; no word-stress location given; 'stress' mentioned only for Spanish loan sources (fn. 27).

sources.citation: Eischens, Ben & Ryan T. Bennett. 2025. The Mixtec couplet is not a consistent grammatical unit. Glossa (doi:10.16995/glossa.18740); lingbuzz/009245 preprint.
sources.note: pp. 11, 13 (preprint): SMP Mixtec has a bimoraic foot right-aligned to the prosodic word; a stress-based alternative ('the penultimate mora of a root is stressed') is raised and left open; rising tones 'are licensed on both morae in the foot, not just the stressed one (whether feet are taken to be trochaic or iambic in SMP Mixtec)' — foot headedness/stress position explicitly undetermined.

sources.citation: DiCanio, Christian & Ryan Bennett. 2018 [2020]. Prosody in Mesoamerican languages. Preprint of chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody.
sources.note: Survey §2.2 Stress: Mixtecan 14 languages surveyed — 7 root-initial, 4 root-final, 3 variable; 'Stress is usually fixed in Oto-Manguean languages, and is always confined to roots/stems'. No west2643 variety is among those surveyed.

sources.note: Nothing on stress (bimoraic minimality only).

sources.note: No SMPM stress statement; the only 'phrasal stress/prominence' passage (p. 8) reports Gerfen 1999 on Coatzospan Mixtec.

sources.citation: Eischens, Ben & Andrew A. Hedding. 2024 [print 2025]. San Martín Peras Mixtec (Illustration of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 54(2): 811–852. doi:10.1017/S0025100324000124
sources.note: Nothing on word stress. §3 'Prosodic features' covers syllable structure/couplet, phonation, lexical tone and tone sandhi; §3.1 (p. 823): 'lexical roots are minimally, and usually maximally, bimoraic... The couplet in SMPM is the locus of phonation contrasts and tonal melodies.' No stress, prominence or foot-headedness statement.
